title: Abel-Ruffini Theorem
description: A pedagogical walkthrough of the Abel-Ruffini theorem (Wiedijk #16) composed from Mathlib's Galois theory infrastructure: the contrapositive chain from solvability by radicals (`IsSolvableByRad`) through solvable Galois groups (`IsSolvable q.Gal`) to the non-solvability of S₅ (since A₅ is simple and non-abelian), organized as 9 theorems across 187 lines with zero sorries and zero axioms. There is no general solution in radicals to polynomial equations of degree five or higher — first proved by Abel (1824) and later illuminated by Galois's theory connecting radical solvability to group structure.

meta.author: Paolo Ruffini (1799, incomplete), Niels Henrik Abel (1824), Évariste Galois (1832, publ. Liouville 1846)

mathlibDependencies.description: Galois's theorem in its computationally useful form: if a polynomial $p \in F[X]$ is solvable by radicals over a field $F$ of characteristic zero, then the Galois group $\mathrm{Gal}(\mathrm{SplittingField}(p)/F)$ is solvable. Mathlib formalizes this via the `solvableByRad` subfield (the smallest subfield closed under radicals) and proves `solvableByRad.isSolvable'` by induction on the radical tower: each radical adjunction is a cyclic Kummer extension whose Galois group is cyclic (hence abelian, hence solvable), and solvability lifts through tower composites via the closure of solvability under extensions. This file consumes the theorem in `galois_bridge` (the canonical wrapper) and in its *contrapositive* form via `not_solvable_by_rad_of_not_solvable_gal` — the abstract Abel-Ruffini obstruction stating that a non-solvable Galois group rules out any radical formula. Composing the contrapositive with `symmetric_group_not_solvable` then yields the classical impossibility for the generic quintic (Galois group $S_5$). This dependency is the *field-theoretic half* of the proof; the group-theoretic half (provided by `Equiv.Perm.not_solvable` below) supplies the unsolvability witness that the contrapositive needs.

The smallest non-abelian simple group: $A_5$ has no nontrivial proper normal subgroups, formalized as `IsSimpleGroup (alternatingGroup (Fin 5))`. Mathlib proves this via the classical 3-cycle conjugacy argument: $A_5$ is generated by 3-cycles, any normal subgroup containing a non-identity element must contain a 3-cycle (case analysis on cycle type — $1{+}1{+}1{+}1{+}1$, $2{+}2{+}1$, $3{+}1{+}1$, $5$), and the 3-cycles form a single conjugacy class in $A_5$. The sibling gallery entries `sylow-theorem-oq-04` and `sylow-theorems-oq-04` give the alternative Sylow-counting derivation ($n_2 = 5$, $n_3 = 10$, $n_5 = 6$ for $|A_5| = 60 = 2^2 \cdot 3 \cdot 5$, conjugacy classes $\{1, 12, 12, 15, 20\}$, no sub-sum dividing 60 starting with 1) that gives the structural content of what Mathlib here delegates to a one-liner. This file invokes the simplicity theorem in `a5_is_simple`, then uses it indirectly through Mathlib's chain `IsSimpleGroup.derivedSeries_eq_bot_iff_isSolvable` → `Equiv.Perm.not_solvable` to mechanize the $n = 5$ non-solvability case. The simplicity of $A_5$ is *the* mathematical content that makes Abel-Ruffini true; everything else in this file is structural plumbing around it.

The non-solvability of $S_n$ for $n \geq 5$, formalized as `¬ IsSolvable (Equiv.Perm (Fin n))` whenever `5 ≤ n`. This file invokes the lemma specifically at $n = 5$ via `symmetric_group_not_solvable` and propagates it through the contrapositive `not_solvable_by_rad_of_not_solvable_gal` to obstruct radical solvability of the generic quintic. Internally Mathlib proves this by showing $\mathrm{derivedSeries}(S_n) \supseteq A_n$ for all $n \geq 5$ — using that $A_n$ is perfect (i.e. $[A_n, A_n] = A_n$) for $n \geq 5$, which in turn uses `alternatingGroup.isSimpleGroup_five` (this file's previous dependency) plus a 3-cycle-conjugacy argument that lifts simplicity to perfection. The full extension to all $n \geq 5$ uses that $A_n$ contains $A_5$ as a subgroup for $n \geq 5$ together with the perfectness of $A_5$. This is the *group-theoretic half* of the Abel-Ruffini obstruction — the one that, composed with `solvableByRad.isSolvable'` (this file's first dependency), yields the impossibility of any radical formula for a quintic with Galois group $S_5$.
The Galois group of a polynomial as the automorphism group of its splitting field

Shafarevich's theorem (1954): every finite solvable group G is realizable as Gal(L/ℚ) for some Galois extension L/ℚ. The positive companion to Abel-Ruffini's negative result — Abel-Ruffini blocks radical solvability for non-solvable Galois groups (S₅), Shafarevich asserts every solvable group does appear. Axiomatized in Lean (full proof requires class field theory, embedding problems, and Brauer groups not in Mathlib) with 7 derived corollaries including S₃, S₄ realizability and the threshold observation that S₅ is the first non-realizable-by-Shafarevich case

Shafarevich feasibility study: axiom-free Lean proof for cyclic groups (via Dirichlet + Galois fixed fields) and coprime products (ℤ/mℤ × ℤ/nℤ ≅ ℤ/(mn)ℤ via CRT). Quantifies the gap to full Shafarevich: linear disjointness of cyclotomic subfields at different primes (~500 lines) for the general abelian case, and embedding problem theory (Brauer groups, Galois cohomology, Tate-Poitou duality) for solvable groups generally — none in Mathlib 2026

Burnside's p^a q^b theorem (1904): every finite group of order p^a · q^b is solvable. Provides the structural reason A₅ (order 60 = 2² · 3 · 5, three distinct primes) is the minimal non-solvable group — Burnside rules out solvability obstructions for orders with at most two prime factors. Phase-2 axiomatization handles trivial cases (a = 0, b = 0, p = q) via Mathlib's IsPGroup → IsNilpotent → IsSolvable chain, the squarefree case (a = b = 1) via IsZGroup.of_squarefree, and axiomatizes the genuinely-open Lean content (a ≥ 2 ∨ b ≥ 2) as `burnside_pq_nontrivial`

Chebotarev density theorem (1922): in a Galois extension L/ℚ with group G, primes distribute among Frobenius conjugacy classes with density |C|/|G|. The computational engine for Galois group determination — converting Abel-Ruffini's abstract impossibility into an effective procedure (factorize f mod a few hundred primes, match cycle-type distribution against transitive-subgroup cycle indices). Axiomatized in Lean with 23 derived results including all S₅ and A₅ conjugacy class sizes (verified by native_decide) and statistical detection of solvability via prime density signatures — directly addresses key insight #18 (Frobenius-Chebotarev) and the openQuestion on Chebotarev formalization

Together with abel-ruffini-oq-04-oq-01 (Gal=S₅ for x⁵−4x+2) and inverse-galois-oq-06 (companion A₅ formalization), provides the gallery's complete inventory of concrete unsolvable-quintic witnesses to which `not_solvable_by_rad_of_not_solvable_gal` can be applied.

D₄ is solvable (derived series D₄ ⊃ ⟨r⟩ ≅ ℤ/4 ⊃ ⟨r²⟩ ≅ ℤ/2 ⊃ {e}), so X⁴−2 IS solvable by radicals — exactly as the converse of `not_solvable_by_rad_of_not_solvable_gal` predicts. Provides a positive concrete instance of the Galois-correspondence side this entry uses contrapositively, with 27 theorems, 0 sorries, 0 axioms.

S2 scaffold for the general dihedral-Galois criterion: 'When is $\text{Gal}(X^n - a/\mathbb{Q})$ dihedral?' Defines `IsDihedralGaloisOfXnMinusA n a` abstractly via Mathlib's `Polynomial.SplittingField` and `DihedralGroup`, states the $(n=4, a=2)$ specialization (recovering `inverse-galois-d4`'s concrete D₄ realization), and the Schinzel-Vélez characterization (1973) — sorry-guarded pending Capelli's irreducibility theorem (absent from Mathlib v4.26.0). **Why this matters for Abel-Ruffini**: the polynomials $X^n - a$ are precisely the *single-radical-step generators* — every radical tower $F = K_0 \subset K_1 \subset \cdots \subset K_m$ adjoins one $\sqrt[n_i]{a_i}$, a root of an $X^{n_i} - a_i$, at each step. Knowing exactly which $X^n - a$ have dihedral Galois groups (vs cyclic, vs Frobenius $F_{20}$ for $X^5 - 2$ in `inverse-galois-f20`, vs more exotic groups) is therefore a *structural classification* of the building blocks Galois's theorem traces through the bridge. Dihedral groups $D_n$ are always solvable (derived series $D_n \supset \langle r \rangle \cong \mathbb{Z}/n \supset \{e\}$ with abelian quotients $\mathbb{Z}/2$ and $\mathbb{Z}/n$), so every $X^n - a$ with dihedral Galois group lies on the *solvable* side of `not_solvable_by_rad_of_not_solvable_gal` — consistent with the manifest radical expressibility of $\sqrt[n]{a}$ itself. The criterion is therefore one piece of the converse-of-Abel-Ruffini implementation: classifying the Galois groups of radical generators so that radical solvability can be witnessed effectively. 11 theorems, 1 sorry, 0 axioms, 235 lines.

Concrete realization of the Frobenius group F₂₀ = ℤ/5 ⋊ ℤ/4 (order 20) as Gal(X⁵−2/ℚ): lower bound 20 | |Gal| from X⁵−2 irreducible (5 | |Gal|) plus Φ₅ irreducible (4 | rank), upper bound from all roots lying in ℚ(⁵√2, ζ₅) of degree ≤ 20. **Crucial clarification of Abel-Ruffini's scope**: X⁵−2 has degree 5 but Gal(X⁵−2/ℚ) ≅ F₂₀ is solvable (F₂₀ ⊃ ℤ/5 ⊃ {e} with abelian quotients), so X⁵−2 IS solvable by radicals (the explicit root is ⁵√2). Abel-Ruffini's impossibility is therefore not about degree alone — it is precisely about which Galois groups are non-solvable. The contrast inverse-galois-f20 (solvable, degree 5) vs abel-ruffini-oq-04-oq-01 (S₅, degree 5) makes the threshold concrete: same degree, different fate, decided by group structure. 27 theorems, 0 sorries, 0 axioms.

Wiedijk #72 — the complete formalization of Sylow's three theorems (existence, conjugacy, counting constraint n_p ≡ 1 (mod p)). Foundational for the simplicity of A₅ that drives Abel-Ruffini's impossibility: the Sylow counting argument for |A₅| = 60 = 2² · 3 · 5 forces n₂ = 5, n₃ = 10, n₅ = 6, all of which exceed 1, hence no Sylow subgroup is normal — the keystone proof of A₅'s simplicity. The Mathlib alternativeGroup.isSimpleGroup_five used in this entry is built on these Sylow theorems. 10 theorems, 0 sorries, 0 axioms.

Classification of groups of order pq via Sylow's theorems: for distinct primes p < q with p ∤ q − 1, every group of order pq is cyclic. This is the simplest non-trivial Sylow classification — all such groups are abelian, hence solvable, and the corresponding polynomials of degree pq have solvable Galois groups whenever realized. Concrete examples of orders 6, 15, 21, 35 are all solvable, in agreement with the converse of `not_solvable_by_rad_of_not_solvable_gal`. The first non-solvable group |A₅| = 60 = 2² · 3 · 5 has three prime factors — outside the pq-classification reach, consistent with A₅ being the minimal Abel-Ruffini obstruction.

This orbit-stabilizer identity is the engine that converts Sylow II/III into the divisibility constraints $n_p \mid |G|/p^{v_p(|G|)}$ and $n_p \equiv 1 \pmod p$ used to compute $n_2 = 5, n_3 = 10, n_5 = 6$ for $A_5$ — the exhaustive enumeration that forces simplicity. Formalizes existence (Zorn's lemma on closed pro-$p$ subgroups), conjugacy (finite-quotient approximation + finite intersection property in compact spaces), and the finite-recovery bridge $\text{IsProP}\ G\ p \Leftrightarrow \text{IsPGroup}\ p\ G$ with 10 theorems, 4 axioms, 0 sorries. The pro-$p$ Sylow subgroups of $G_{\mathbb{Q}}$ — the Galois groups of maximal pro-$p$ extensions $\mathbb{Q}^{(p)}/\mathbb{Q}$ — control its $p$-primary structure, exactly as finite Sylow $p$-subgroups control finite groups. Together with class field theory's classification of $G_{\mathbb{Q}}^{\text{ab}}$ via idèle class quotients (keyInsight #12), they form the structural lineage from Abel-Ruffini's finite-group obstruction to the modern arithmetic of number fields.

Cantor's 1874 theorem that the algebraic closure ℚ̄ is countable (|ℚ̄| = ℵ₀) via degree-by-degree enumeration of ℚ[X], each polynomial having finitely many roots. Sits one tier above Abel-Ruffini in the algebraic-vs-radical-vs-transcendental hierarchy: ℚ̄ is countable, but the *radically expressible* sub-subset is a strict (still countable) subset, and Abel-Ruffini exhibits explicit elements of ℚ̄ (roots of x⁵ − 4x + 2) that escape it. Combined with |ℝ| = 2^ℵ₀, Cantor's countability gives the existence of transcendentals (cf. `liouville-theorem`); Abel-Ruffini delivers a parallel impossibility one tier down — algebraic non-radicals exist among the countable ℚ̄. The implications section's 'impossibility paradigm' (#7) and 'transcendence hierarchy' (#8) place both results on the same Galois-(1832)–Cantor-(1874)–Lindemann-(1882) lineage of cardinality- and expressibility-based barriers.

Together the trio (Wiedijk #16 + #22 + #63) anchor the algebraic, cardinal, and abstract-categorical corners of the gallery's diagonal-and-impossibility methodology.

Liouville's 1844 explicit construction of transcendental numbers (e.g. $\sum_{k=1}^{\infty} 10^{-k!}$) via the rational-approximation bound $|\alpha - p/q| > C/q^n$ for algebraic $\alpha$ of degree $n$. Sits one tier above Abel-Ruffini in the expressibility hierarchy this entry's implications section traces: the chain $\mathbb{Q} \subsetneq \overline{\mathbb{Q}}_{\text{rad}} \subsetneq \overline{\mathbb{Q}} \subsetneq \mathbb{C}$ has Abel-Ruffini blocking $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}_{\text{rad}} \subsetneq \overline{\mathbb{Q}}$ (algebraic numbers without radical expressions, via $S_5$ non-solvability) and Liouville blocking $\overline{\mathbb{Q}} \subsetneq \mathbb{C}$ (transcendentals beyond every polynomial equation, via Diophantine approximation). The two together with Hermite-Lindemann ($e, \pi$ transcendental, 1873/1882) form the historical sequence Galois (1832) → Liouville (1844) → Cantor (1874) → Hermite-Lindemann (1882) of expressibility-and-cardinality barriers.

Hermite-Lindemann theorem (Hermite 1873 for $e$; Lindemann 1882 for $e^\alpha$ with $\alpha \in \overline{\mathbb{Q}} \setminus \{0\}$; Wiedijk #56): for every nonzero algebraic $\alpha$, the value $e^\alpha$ is transcendental, immediately yielding $e$ transcendental ($\alpha = 1$, Wiedijk #67) and $\pi$ transcendental ($e^{i\pi} = -1$ algebraic, so $i\pi$ must be transcendental, hence $\pi$, Wiedijk #53). **The top rung of the expressibility hierarchy this entry's implications section explicitly traces** (#8: 'TRANSCENDENCE HIERARCHY: Abel-Ruffini's impossibility … sits between irrationality ($\sqrt{2} \notin \mathbb{Q}$, c. 500 BCE) and transcendence ($e, \pi \notin \overline{\mathbb{Q}}$, 1882)'): where Abel-Ruffini blocks $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}_{\text{rad}} \subsetneq \overline{\mathbb{Q}}$ (algebraic-non-radical, via $S_5$ non-solvability) and Liouville-1844 exhibits a constructive transcendental separating $\overline{\mathbb{Q}} \subsetneq \mathbb{C}$ by Diophantine approximation, Hermite-Lindemann supplies the *natural-constants* witnesses $e, \pi$ for the same outer separation — replacing Liouville's artificial $\sum 10^{-k!}$ with two ubiquitous mathematical constants and thereby resolving the ancient circle-squaring problem (Lindemann 1882). **Methodologically parallel to Abel-Ruffini**: both are *impossibility theorems* with structurally identical three-step templates — translate the expressibility question to a structural invariant of a field extension (Galois group solvability for Abel-Ruffini; algebraic dependence over $\mathbb{Q}$ for Hermite-Lindemann), characterize the class admitting expressibility (solvable Galois groups; algebraic numbers), then exhibit a violating instance ($x^5 - 4x + 2$ with $\text{Gal} = S_5$ in `abel-ruffini-oq-04-oq-01`; $e^\alpha$ for any nonzero algebraic $\alpha$ via Hermite's auxiliary-polynomial method, an integer-vs-analytic-bound contradiction). Hermite-Lindemann thus extends the Wantzel-Galois methodological lineage (keyInsight #24 of this entry) from radicals to elementary functions: the auxiliary-polynomial / integer-bound contradiction is the *transcendence-theory* analog of Abel-Ruffini's derived-series / non-solvable-group obstruction. The gallery formalization (390 lines, 1 axiom — `hermite_lindemann` itself, plus 4 derived corollaries including $e$ transcendence and $\pi$ transcendence via Euler's identity) is the upper end of the expressibility-barrier chain whose lower end (`not_solvable_by_rad_of_not_solvable_gal`) is proved fully axiom-free here.

Burnside's lemma (Cauchy 1845, Frobenius 1887, Burnside 1897): $|X/G| = \frac{1}{|G|}\sum_{g \in G} |\text{Fix}(g)|$. The orbit-side companion of the cycle-index polynomial $Z(H; p_1, \ldots, p_n) = \frac{1}{|H|}\sum_{h \in H} \prod_j p_j^{c_j(h)}$ that drives algorithmic Galois-group identification: factorize $f \bmod p$ and match the empirical cycle-type distribution against $\{Z(H) : H \leq S_n \text{ transitive}\}$ via Chebotarev density — the procedure underlying Stauduhar's algorithm and modern `polgalois` implementations. Foundational substrate for keyInsights #18 (Frobenius-Chebotarev) and #17 (LMFDB statistical fingerprinting) and to the openQuestion on Chebotarev formalization.

The master Inverse Galois Problem entry (1882 lines, 5 axioms, 0 sorries): explicit Galois group realizations for 23 finite groups, including the first non-solvable case A₅ via Gal(x⁵ − 5x⁴ + 10x³ − 10x² + 25x − 5/ℚ) (Sylow-theoretic order analysis with Vandermonde discriminant argument over ℂ and the Sophie Germain identity), D₄ via X⁴ − 2, F₂₀ via X⁵ − 2, and a systematic census of all groups of order ≤ 8 via cyclotomic fields ℚ(ζₙ). The positive companion to Abel-Ruffini's negative result: Abel-Ruffini shows non-solvable Galois groups (S₅, A₅) obstruct radical solvability; inverse-galois exhibits explicit polynomials over ℚ realizing each obstruction. Together with `inverse-galois-a5`, `inverse-galois-d4`, `inverse-galois-f20` (all individually cross-referenced), this entry frames the gallery's complete realizability landscape: every concrete Galois group whose non-solvability is invoked by `not_solvable_by_rad_of_not_solvable_gal` is realized as Gal(q/ℚ) for an explicit q here.

Non-solvable frontier of the Inverse Galois Problem: proves the bidirectional characterization Sₙ solvable ⟺ n ≤ 4 and Aₙ solvable ⟺ n ≤ 4, formalizes A₅ simple ∧ perfect ∧ not solvable, and establishes the FTGT-derived quotient realizability theorem (every quotient of a realized Galois group is itself realized). Provides the exact threshold companion to this entry's `symmetric_group_not_solvable n hn`: where Abel-Ruffini stops at the one-directional ¬IsSolvable(Sₙ) for n ≥ 5, `inverse-galois-oq-01` adds the converse IsSolvable(Sₙ) for n ≤ 4 (filling Mathlib's missing S₂, S₃, S₄ instances) and the perfection statement [A₅, A₅] = A₅ that makes the derived-series obstruction precise. Includes Cayley's embedding G ↪ S|G| linking abstract group realizability to the symmetric-group picture this entry uses.

Pólya enumeration theorem (PET) for cyclic groups: $n \cdot (\#\text{distinct } k\text{-necklaces}) = \sum_{d \mid n} \varphi(n/d) \cdot k^d$, refining Burnside's lemma by recording per-element fixed-point counts via the cycle-index polynomial. The combinatorial analogue of the cycle-index identification underlying algorithmic Galois-group detection (referenced in `burnside-counting`): just as PET decomposes orbit counts via cycle structure over $C_n$, Stauduhar-type Galois detection decomposes the Frobenius cycle-type distribution over transitive subgroups of $S_n$. Concretely verified for binary 4-necklaces: $2^4 + 2^1 + 2^2 + 2^1 = 24$, giving 6 distinct necklaces — the same enumerative engine that, applied to $S_5$'s transitive subgroup lattice (5 groups: $C_5, D_5, F_{20}, A_5, S_5$), produces the cycle-type signatures used to distinguish solvable ($C_5, D_5, F_{20}$) from non-solvable ($A_5, S_5$) quintic Galois groups.

Mathieu group $M_{23}$ (order $|M_{23}| = 2^7 \cdot 3^2 \cdot 5 \cdot 7 \cdot 11 \cdot 23 = 10{,}200{,}960$), the unique sporadic simple group whose realizability as $\text{Gal}(L/\mathbb{Q})$ remains open in 2026. Formalizes that $M_{23}$ is perfect ($[M_{23}, M_{23}] = M_{23}$), non-solvable, and beyond the reach of Shafarevich's theorem (which classifies only the solvable case). Directly extends this entry's openQuestion on the Inverse Galois Problem: where Abel-Ruffini exhibits $S_5$ as the smallest non-solvable Galois group obstructing radical solvability, $M_{23}$ marks the current frontier of the inverse direction — every other finite simple group (the four infinite families $\mathbb{Z}/p$, $A_n$, classical Lie type, exceptional Lie type, plus 25 of the 26 sporadics) has been realized over $\mathbb{Q}$ via rigidity, Belyi covers, or Thompson-style triples. $M_{23}$'s six-prime order (vs $A_5$'s three primes) and lack of a known $\mathbb{Q}$-rational rigid triple keep it stubbornly outside the constructive RIGP toolkit.

Hilbert's 12th Problem (Kronecker's Jugendtraum, 1880): extend the Kronecker-Weber theorem to arbitrary number fields by finding explicit transcendental functions whose special values generate all abelian extensions. The positive complement to Abel-Ruffini's negative result at the *abelian* extreme of the Galois-group spectrum: where Kronecker-Weber (1853/1886/1896) explicitly generates every abelian extension of $\mathbb{Q}$ via roots of unity $\zeta_n = e^{2\pi i/n}$ (radical-expressible by definition), Hilbert's 12th asks for the analogous explicit generators over an arbitrary base — fully resolved only for imaginary quadratic fields via the $j$-invariant and Weber functions of CM elliptic curves (the original Kronecker Jugendtraum, completed by Takagi 1920 and Hasse 1930). Implications #3 of this entry places Abel-Ruffini at the threshold between (a) abelian extensions (Kronecker-Weber-classifiable, radically solvable) and (c) non-solvable extensions ($A_5$-blocked, the present entry's obstruction); Hilbert 12 / Jugendtraum addresses the same abelian-classification question one base-field shift up, completing the positive arithmetic-program companion to the negative impossibility theorem.

The cubic-degree concrete Galois group computation companion: machine-verifies $|\text{Gal}(8X^3 - 6X - 1/\mathbb{Q})| = 3$ — the minimal polynomial of $\cos(20°)$ — via Eisenstein-on-shifted-polynomial irreducibility ($X^3 - 6X^2 + 9X - 3$ Eisenstein at $p = 3$) plus the observation that all three roots $\{\cos(20°), \cos(100°), \cos(220°)\}$ lie in $\mathbb{Q}(\alpha)$ (the splitting field equals the simple extension because the three roots are polynomial expressions in any one of them via Chebyshev triple-angle). The Galois group is $\mathbb{Z}/3\mathbb{Z}$, which is solvable (trivially — every cyclic group is) so $\cos(20°)$ *is* solvable by radicals: Cardano's formula gives $\cos(20°) = \frac{1}{2}\left(\sqrt[3]{\frac{1 + i\sqrt{3}}{2}} + \sqrt[3]{\frac{1 - i\sqrt{3}}{2}}\right)$, the canonical *casus irreducibilis* (cf. keyInsight #29) requiring complex cube roots even though the answer is real. The contrast with Abel-Ruffini's quintic obstruction is sharp: cubic Galois groups are subgroups of $S_3$ (orders 1, 2, 3, 6 — all solvable), so Cardano 1545 succeeds; quintic Galois groups include $S_5$ (order 120, non-solvable), so no analogue exists. The angle-trisection cubic also exhibits the Wantzel/Galois split (keyInsight #24): solvability by radicals ($|\text{Gal}| = 3$ solvable, so radicals exist) is distinct from constructibility ($|\text{Gal}| \neq 2^k$, so compass-and-straightedge fails) — angle-trisection of $60°$ is radically solvable but geometrically impossible. The sibling entries `angle-trisection-cos-20-gal-oq-01` ($\cos(\pi/7)$, $|\text{Gal}| = 3$), `angle-trisection-cos-20-gal-oq-03` ($\cos(40°)$, $|\text{Gal}| = 3$), `angle-trisection-cos-20-gal-oq-03-oq-01` ($\cos(72°)$, $|\text{Gal}| = 2$), and `angle-trisection-cos-20-gal-oq-01-oq-01` (parameterized cubic across $p \in \{3, 7\}$) extend the picture across the gallery's cubic-Galois landscape. Open question #7 of this entry cites all five computations as the cubic-level baseline against which the unformalized $x^5 - x - 1 \Rightarrow \text{Gal} = S_5$ Selmer-style computation must rise — 0 sorries, 0 axioms across the family.

The **closed-form generalization** of the per-prime cubic Galois computations in the $\cos(\pi/n)$ family: machine-verifies the *uniform* formula $|\text{Gal}(\text{minpoly}_{\mathbb{Q}}(\cos(\pi/n)))| = \varphi(2n)/2$ for every $n \geq 3$ via Mathlib's `IsCyclotomicExtension` infrastructure (0 axioms, 0 sorries, 12 theorems, 338 lines). The reduction $\cos(\pi/n) = \cos(2\pi/(2n))$ identifies $\mathbb{Q}(\cos(\pi/n))$ with the maximal real subfield $\mathbb{Q}(\zeta_{2n})^+$ of the $(2n)$-th cyclotomic field, whose Galois group $(\mathbb{Z}/2n\mathbb{Z})^\times / \{\pm 1\}$ has order $\varphi(2n)/2$ — abelian (hence solvable) for all $n$. **Why this matters for Abel-Ruffini's framing**: the entry's cross-referenced $\cos(\pi/n)$ instances — `angle-trisection-cos-20-gal` ($n=9$, $\varphi(18)/2 = 3$, since $\cos(20°) = \cos(\pi/9)$), `angle-trisection-cos-20-gal-oq-01` ($n=7$, $\varphi(14)/2 = 3$), `angle-trisection-cos-20-gal-oq-01-oq-02` ($n=5$, $\varphi(10)/2 = 2$, since $\cos(36°) = \cos(\pi/5)$) — are now corollaries of a single uniform statement, replacing case-by-case Eisenstein computations with the cyclotomic field's structural classification. The $\cos(2\pi/n)$ siblings (`angle-trisection-cos-20-gal-oq-03` for $\cos(40°) = \cos(2\pi/9)$ and `angle-trisection-cos-20-gal-oq-03-oq-01` for $\cos(72°) = \cos(2\pi/5)$) generate the same fields $\mathbb{Q}(\zeta_n)^+$ as their $\cos(\pi/n)$ counterparts and admit the parallel formula $\varphi(n)/2$ from the same cyclotomic theory. Every minimal polynomial in either family thus lies on the **solvable side** of `not_solvable_by_rad_of_not_solvable_gal` because abelian Galois groups are tautologically solvable (derived series terminates in one step). The contrast with the quintic case sharpens: cos-of-rational-multiples-of-$\pi$ Galois groups are *always* abelian by cyclotomic theory, so this entire infinite family is radically solvable — Galois groups containing $A_5$ as a composition factor (the Abel-Ruffini obstruction) cannot arise here. This generalization also makes precise the connection between Wantzel's 1837 constructibility criterion (keyInsight #24) and the Gauss-1801 Disquisitiones classification: a regular $n$-gon is compass-straightedge constructible iff $\varphi(n)$ is a power of $2$, i.e., iff $n = 2^k \prod p_i$ with each $p_i$ a Fermat prime — a uniform group-order computation rather than per-$n$ irreducibility analysis. Companion to the still-sorry-1 `angle-trisection-cos-20-gal-oq-01-oq-03` (Eisenstein-at-$p$ conjecture for the $\cos(\pi/p)$ family) which carries the same structural content along the irreducibility axis.

Cardano's 1545 cubic formula — the degree-3 case where the radical strategy succeeds, formalized in Lean. The Galois bridge places this on the solvable side of `not_solvable_by_rad_of_not_solvable_gal`: every cubic has Galois group a subgroup of $S_3$, and $S_3$ is solvable (derived series $S_3 \supset A_3 \supset \{e\}$ with abelian quotients $\mathbb{Z}/2$ and $\mathbb{Z}/3$ — derived length 2, matching Cardano's two nested radicals $\sqrt{\cdot}$ inside $\sqrt[3]{\cdot}$). Together with `general-quartic` (Ferrari 1545, derived length 3) and the impossibility threshold proved here at degree 5, this entry completes the historical triptych: cubic-quartic-quintic, the three classical case-studies that motivated the 300-year search for the quintic formula whose impossibility this file's `not_solvable_by_rad_of_not_solvable_gal` formalizes.

Ferrari's 1545 quartic formula — the *last* degree where the radical strategy succeeds. The Galois bridge places this on the solvable side of `not_solvable_by_rad_of_not_solvable_gal`: $S_4$ has the composition series $S_4 \supset A_4 \supset V_4 \supset \langle(12)(34)\rangle \supset \{e\}$ with abelian quotients $\mathbb{Z}/2, \mathbb{Z}/3, \mathbb{Z}/2, \mathbb{Z}/2$ (derived length 3, matching the four nested radicals — one square, one cube, two squares — in Ferrari's formula via the resolvent cubic; see keyInsight #4). The Klein four-group $V_4 \trianglelefteq S_4$ is the *crucial* normal subgroup whose absence at degree 5 forces Abel-Ruffini: $A_5$ has no analogous normal subgroup because $A_5$ is simple non-abelian. `general-quartic` is therefore the immediate classical predecessor whose Galois-theoretic success ends at the exact threshold proved unattainable here for $n \geq 5$.

Cardano-Ferrari resolvent bridge, formalized. Machine-verifies the explicit algebraic reduction by which Ferrari's quartic method invokes Cardano's cubic formula: the Tschirnhaus substitution $m = t - 5p/6$ transforms Ferrari's resolvent cubic into depressed form $m^3 + Pm + Q = 0$, so Cardano's formula directly supplies the resolvent root that completes the quartic solution (9 theorems, 0 sorries, 0 axioms). This is the concrete Lean-verified instance of the $S_4 / V_4 \cong S_3$ Galois quotient (keyInsight #4) at the level of explicit formulas — the cubic-quartic interplay made manifest as polynomial algebra rather than abstract group theory. Historically it captures the *last* successful resolvent reduction before Abel-Ruffini's threshold: the chain quadratic→cubic (degree-2 resolvent) → cubic→quartic (degree-3 resolvent, formalized here) terminates at the next step, where Lagrange's 1770 calculation showed the quintic's natural resolvent has degree 6 > 5 so no analogous reduction reaches a lower-degree problem. The progression Cardano (1545) → Ferrari (1545) → `solution-of-cubic-oq-05` (Lean formalization of their interplay) → `not_solvable_by_rad_of_not_solvable_gal` (impossibility threshold proved here) traces precisely how the radical strategy succeeds twice and then fails, sharpening the abstract derived-series picture of `solution-of-cubic` and `general-quartic` with the explicit algebraic-bridge formalization.

**The existence theorem complementary to Abel-Ruffini's expressibility obstruction — Wiedijk #2 paired with Wiedijk #16.** Gauss's 1799 theorem (Wiedijk #2): every non-constant $p \in \mathbb{C}[X]$ has at least one complex root, equivalently $\mathbb{C}$ is algebraically closed. Abel-Ruffini (1824, Wiedijk #16, the present entry): roots of generic degree-$\geq 5$ polynomials over $\mathbb{Q}$ are not expressible by radicals. The two results carve mathematically orthogonal directions: **existence vs expressibility**. FTA guarantees the five roots of $x^5 - 4x + 2$ *exist* in $\mathbb{C}$ (so the equation is solvable in the loose sense of having a solution set); Abel-Ruffini, via `not_solvable_by_rad_of_not_solvable_gal` applied to $\text{Gal}(x^5 - 4x + 2/\mathbb{Q}) \cong S_5$ (formalized in `abel-ruffini-oq-04-oq-01`), shows those five roots admit *no closed-form expression* in radicals over $\mathbb{Q}$. The pairing makes precise what Part VII point 4 of this entry's Lean docstring calls *'the contrast with numerics'*: the quintic has solutions (FTA gives existence and numerical computability), but the solutions cannot be written symbolically via $+, -, \times, \div, \sqrt[n]{\,}$. Methodologically the two theorems sit at opposite ends of the analysis-vs-algebra spectrum: FTA's standard proofs are topological (winding-number arguments, Liouville's theorem on bounded entire functions, the maximum modulus principle) while Abel-Ruffini's is purely algebraic (Galois groups, derived series, simplicity of $A_5$). The Lean gallery houses both: `fundamental-theorem-algebra` (Wiedijk #2) formalizes Gauss's existence theorem via Mathlib's `Complex.isAlgClosed`, the abstract closure of $\mathbb{C}$ under algebraic equations; `abel-ruffini` formalizes the expressibility obstruction. Together they verify the *complete* Wiedijk-flavored picture of polynomial equations over $\mathbb{Q}$: roots exist by FTA, are countable by `algebraic-numbers-countable` (Cantor 1874), but generically escape radical expressibility by Abel-Ruffini. The trichotomy is captured by the keyInsight #14 hierarchy $\mathbb{Q} \subsetneq \overline{\mathbb{Q}}_{\text{rad}} \subsetneq \overline{\mathbb{Q}} \subsetneq \mathbb{C}$: FTA fills in $\overline{\mathbb{Q}} \subsetneq \mathbb{C}$ on the *positive* (root-existence) side, while Abel-Ruffini sharpens $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}_{\text{rad}} \subsetneq \overline{\mathbb{Q}}$ on the *negative* (radical-expressibility) side.

**The constructibility-side biconditional of Abel-Ruffini's solvability bridge — Wantzel-Galois in Mathlib.** This entry formalizes the constructibility analog of `galois_bridge`/`not_solvable_by_rad_of_not_solvable_gal`: it proves that for every irreducible $p \in \mathbb{Q}[X]$, $\text{natDegree}(p) \mid |\text{Gal}(p)|$ (a uniform generalization of Mathlib's prime-degree-only `Polynomial.natDegree_dvd_card_galois_group_of_irreducible_prime_degree`), and uses it to derive that 2-group Galois groups force degree to be a power of 2 — the Wantzel-Galois constructibility criterion (compass-and-straightedge expressibility $\iff$ Galois group is a 2-group, cf. keyInsight #24 on Wantzel 1837). The structural parallel to this entry is exact and bidirectional: where `not_solvable_by_rad_of_not_solvable_gal` here translates *radical*-expressibility into a structural invariant of $\text{Gal}(q)$ (solvability), `angle-trisection-oq-02-oq-01` translates *constructible*-expressibility into the same kind of invariant ($2$-group structure). The two biconditionals together fix the precise Galois-theoretic content of *expressibility-by-elementary-operations* for two different operation classes: $\{+, -, \times, \div, \sqrt[n]{\,}\}$ (this entry, $\iff$ solvable $\text{Gal}$) versus $\{+, -, \times, \div, \sqrt{\,}\}$ (Wantzel-Galois, $\iff$ 2-group $\text{Gal}$). The strict containment 2-group $\subsetneq$ solvable group is then the strict containment constructibility $\subsetneq$ radical solvability: $\sqrt[3]{2}$ is radically expressible (Cardano gives the cube root directly) but *not* constructible ($[\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt[3]{2}):\mathbb{Q}] = 3$, not a power of 2). The gallery entry achievement: by sharpening Mathlib's prime-only natDegree-divides-Galois-order lemma to all irreducibles, it eliminates one axiom from the parent Wantzel-Galois formalization `angle-trisection-oq-02` — a direct Lean-mathlib infrastructure contribution complementing this entry's pedagogical-wrapper approach. Companion entries `angle-trisection`, `angle-trisection-oq-02`, `angle-trisection-cos-20-gal`, and the cubic-Galois sub-entries collectively realize the Wantzel branch of the constructibility/radical-solvability split, structurally mirroring this entry's quintic branch.

**The continuous-superposition analog of Abel-Ruffini's algebraic threshold — Hilbert's 1900 conjecture, resolved by Kolmogorov-Arnold 1956-57.** Hilbert (1900, *Mathematische Probleme*, Göttingen Lecture) asked whether the roots of the *generic* degree-7 polynomial $x^7 + ax^3 + bx^2 + cx + 1 = 0$ — the form after a Tschirnhaus reduction (cf. keyInsight #33) — can be expressed as a *superposition* of continuous functions of 2 variables. This is the *function-composition* analog of Abel-Ruffini's *radical-composition* impossibility: where Abel-Ruffini asks 'is the polynomial root expressible by $\{+, -, \times, \div, \sqrt[n]{\,}\}$?' Hilbert's 13th asks 'is the root expressible by superposition of $C^0$ functions of fewer variables?'. **Kolmogorov-Arnold theorem (Kolmogorov 1956, *Dokl. Akad. Nauk SSSR* 108: 179–182; Arnold 1957, *Dokl. Akad. Nauk SSSR* 114: 679–681)** disproves the conjecture in the *continuous* class: every continuous function of $n$ variables on $[0,1]^n$ admits a representation as a superposition of $2n+1$ continuous functions of *one* variable. The threshold $2n+1$ is sharp (Sternfeld 1985, cross-reference `hilbert-13-oq-04`), structurally parallel to Abel-Ruffini's sharp threshold $n \leq 4$ vs $n \geq 5$. **The methodological coincidence**: V. I. Arnold is the namesake of *both* the 1963 topological proof of Abel-Ruffini (keyInsight #15, monodromy of the discriminant complement) *and* the 1957 Kolmogorov-Arnold superposition theorem — the same mathematical instinct (pinning *algebraic* expressibility obstructions to *topological* invariants) drives both results. **The unresolved algebraic version of Hilbert's 13th**: whether the *algebraic* roots of the generic degree-7 polynomial are expressible by *algebraic* functions of fewer variables remains open (the *algebraic Hilbert 13th*, cf. Arnold-Shimura 1976, Khovanskii 2004). The Kolmogorov-Arnold positive resolution applies only to the continuous-function class; the radical-tower / Tschirnhaus / Bring-Jerrard machinery of this entry (keyInsights #14, #33) shows the generic quintic admits a 1-variable Bring radical representation (reducing 4-parameter to 1-parameter), but the analogous reductions for degree 6 and 7 — *Bring-Jerrard for higher degrees* — remain open. The structural parallel between Abel-Ruffini and Hilbert-13 is therefore *complete on the positive side* (radical $\to$ Bring reduction, continuous $\to$ Kolmogorov-Arnold superposition) and *partially open on the negative side* (Abel-Ruffini's negative content for degree $\geq 5$ is fully proved; Hilbert-13's negative content in the algebraic regime is unresolved).

**The canonical counterexample to Lagrange's converse — and the structural reason $S_4$'s composition series passes through $V_4$ rather than a subgroup of order 6.** Machine-verifies (0 axioms, 0 sorries, 121 lines, exhaustive `native_decide` over all $2^{12} = 4096$ subsets of $A_4$) that $A_4$, despite having order 12 and 6 dividing 12, contains *no* subgroup of order 6. **Why this matters for Abel-Ruffini's threshold**: keyInsight #2 of this entry traces the derived-series chain $S_4 \supset A_4 \supset V_4 \supset \{e\}$ with derived length 3 (the structural reason quartics admit Ferrari's 1545 formula), and keyInsight #4 makes this the *Ferrari resolvent cubic* bridge via $S_4 / V_4 \cong S_3$. The intermediate step $A_4 \supset V_4$ — passing through a *normal* subgroup of order 4 rather than an order-6 subgroup — is *forced* by this non-existence: had $A_4$ contained any subgroup of order 6 (necessarily of index 2, hence normal), the composition factors of $A_4$ could have been $\{2, 3\}$ rather than $\{3, 2, 2\}$, and the entire $V_4$-based machinery of Ferrari's resolvent (Cardano-Ferrari cubic-resolvent technique reducing a quartic to a cubic plus a square root) would have a structurally different organization. The non-existence theorem thus *certifies* the unique pathway $A_4 \supset V_4$ that the abelian-quotient analysis of solvability traces. **The contrast with $A_5$**: where $A_4$ violates Lagrange's converse at the single missing-divisor 6 (still solvable through the Klein-four detour), $A_5$ violates it for *every* proper nontrivial divisor of 60 — there are no proper nontrivial normal subgroups at any order, certifying $A_5$ simple (Mathlib's `alternatingGroup.isSimpleGroup_five`, line 95 here). The two violations form a spectrum: $A_4$ has *some* missing subgroups (Lagrange's converse fails locally at order 6) but the remaining subgroup lattice still admits a normal chain of abelian quotients (Klein four, cyclic-3, trivial); $A_5$ has missing subgroups so densely that *no* proper nontrivial normal subgroup exists. The exhaustive `native_decide` machinery here (4096-subset enumeration) is therefore the finite-case microcosm of the Sylow-counting / orbit-class-equation machinery (cross-references `sylow-theorem-oq-04`, `sylow-theorems-oq-04`) that resolves the $A_5$ case structurally.

**Gauss-Wantzel theorem (Gauss 1801 + Wantzel 1837): the regular $n$-gon is compass-and-straightedge constructible iff $\varphi(n)$ is a power of 2** — the *positive* complement to Abel-Ruffini's negative impossibility, formalized in the gallery with 0 axioms, 0 sorries across 1799 lines and 67+ theorems, including explicit constructibility verdicts for 16 polygons ($n \in \{3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 10, 12, 15, 17, 20, 34, 51, 85, 255, 257, 65537\}$, all of which factor as $2^k \prod p_i$ with $p_i$ distinct Fermat primes) and non-constructibility for 9 ($n \in \{7, 9, 11, 13, 14, 18, 21, 25, 35\}$). **The methodological lineage Abel-Ruffini $\to$ Wantzel-1837 explicitly traced in this entry's keyInsight #24**: Galois (1832) shows radical-solvability $\iff$ solvable Galois group; Wantzel (1837, just *five years later*) restricts the same field-extension machinery to the more demanding compass-straightedge operations (no $n$th roots for $n \geq 3$ — only successive square roots and rational operations) and obtains constructibility $\iff$ Galois group of the splitting field is a 2-group $\iff$ $[\mathbb{Q}(\alpha):\mathbb{Q}]$ is a power of 2. **The chain Abel-Ruffini $\subsetneq$ Wantzel**: every constructible number is radically expressible (square roots are the simplest radicals), but the strict containment is witnessed by $\sqrt[3]{2}$ — radically expressible (Cardano) but *not* constructible ($[\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt[3]{2}):\mathbb{Q}] = 3$, not a power of 2). Equivalently: Galois groups of constructibility are the 2-groups (which are nilpotent, hence solvable); Galois groups of radical solvability are the solvable groups (which strictly include 2-groups by the dihedral $D_p$ for odd primes $p$, all solvable but not 2-groups). **The Fermat-prime corollary linking Gauss-Disquisitiones to Abel-Ruffini**: $\varphi(n)$ a power of 2 forces every odd prime factor of $n$ to be a Fermat prime $F_k = 2^{2^k} + 1$ — Gauss (1801, *Disquisitiones Arithmeticae* §VII) solved $x^{17} - 1 = 0$ in radicals (Galois group $(\mathbb{Z}/17\mathbb{Z})^\times \cong \mathbb{Z}/16\mathbb{Z}$, a 2-group, hence constructible — keyInsight-historical-context tie-in with Vandermonde's 1770 cyclotomic resolvent), and Wantzel's 1837 negative-direction completion shows $x^7 - 1 = 0$ has $\mathbb{Q}(\zeta_7) / \mathbb{Q}$ of degree 6 (not a power of 2), so the regular heptagon is not constructible — the *direct* descendant of Abel-Ruffini's impossibility-via-Galois-structure paradigm. Companion entries `angle-trisection-oq-02-oq-04` (three-level hierarchy: degree-criterion $\Leftarrow$ Galois 2-group $\Leftrightarrow$ tower-criterion) and `angle-trisection-oq-02-oq-01` (Wantzel-Galois biconditional in Mathlib via natDegree_dvd_card) complete the constructibility tier of the gallery's expressibility hierarchy.

**Newton-Girard identities for $k = 4, 5$: the algebraic substrate of Vieta's formulas, Lagrange's 1770 resolvent, and the symmetric-function side of Abel-Ruffini.** Formalizes (0 axioms, 0 sorries, 133 lines) the recurrence $p_4 = e_1 p_3 - e_2 p_2 + e_3 p_1 - 4 e_4$ and $p_5 = e_1 p_4 - e_2 p_3 + e_3 p_2 - e_4 p_1 + 5 e_5$ over arbitrary commutative rings, with dual forms expressing $e_4, e_5$ in terms of power sums $p_1, \ldots, p_5$. **Why this matters for Abel-Ruffini at degree 5**: keyInsight #30 of this entry (*Newton's Identities & the Fundamental Theorem of Symmetric Polynomials*) makes the substrate explicit — every symmetric polynomial in the roots is a polynomial in the elementary symmetrics $e_1, \ldots, e_n$ (equivalently, the coefficients of the polynomial via Vieta's formulas, `vietas-formulas` cross-reference), and the Newton-Girard identities provide the *explicit* transition matrix between the elementary-symmetric basis $\{e_k\}$ and the power-sum basis $\{p_k\}$. The degree-5 case proved in this entry is the algebraic *exact* level at which Abel-Ruffini's obstruction first bites: Lagrange's 1770 resolvent (historicalContext lines 13-15) constructs auxiliary polynomials whose roots are *specific symmetric functions of the roots* of the original; for degree $\leq 4$ the resolvent has degree strictly less than the original (Lagrange's reduction trick — quadratic $\to$ trivial, cubic $\to$ quadratic-in-discriminant, quartic $\to$ resolvent cubic), but for degree 5 the resolvent has degree 6 (Lagrange's own discovery, the *first* concrete evidence of an obstruction), making the explicit Newton-Girard-for-$k = 5$ transformation matrix here the *concrete computational vehicle* of the failed reduction. **The structural parallel to Cayley's resolvent sextic (keyInsight #28)**: where Cayley's 1861 sextic is the *factorization* test for quintic solvability — the resolvent factors over $\mathbb{Q}$ iff $\text{Gal} \leq F_{20}$ — Newton-Girard at $k = 5$ is the *algebra* underlying the resolvent itself, providing the explicit expressions in elementary symmetrics that Cayley's degree-6 polynomial then tests for solvability. Companion `vietas-formulas-oq-03-oq-05` (already cross-referenced) provides the Vieta-formula direction; `amgm-inequality-oq-02-oq-01-oq-02-oq-01-oq-01` is the *power-sum dual* completing the symmetric-function infrastructure that makes Abel-Ruffini's *degree-5 specificity* algebraically explicit rather than abstract group-theoretic.

overview.historicalContext:
The quest to solve polynomial equations drove mathematics for centuries. Quadratic equations were solved in antiquity, cubic equations by Cardano (1545), and quartic equations by Ferrari (1545). For 300 years, mathematicians sought a quintic formula. Joseph-Louis Lagrange's 1770 *Réflexions sur la résolution algébrique des équations* was the crucial precursor: he analyzed why the classical formulas for degrees 2–4 worked by studying permutations of roots ('resolvents'), and noticed that his method broke down for degree 5 — the resolvent of a quintic had degree 6, not lower.

In parallel, Alexandre-Théophile Vandermonde's *Mémoire sur la résolution des équations* (presented to the Académie in 1770, published in 1771) developed similar resolvent ideas independently and applied them with striking success to the cyclotomic equation $x^{11} - 1 = 0$, exhibiting an explicit radical formula for the eleventh roots of unity. Vandermonde's calculation — which today is recognized as a discrete Fourier transform over $\mathbb{Z}/11\mathbb{Z}$ — was the first concrete example of a polynomial of degree above 4 being solved by radicals via group-theoretic considerations. It directly anticipated Gauss's 1801 *Disquisitiones Arithmeticae* §VII, where the constructibility of the regular 17-gon was reduced to solving $x^{17} - 1 = 0$ by radicals via the cyclic structure of $(\mathbb{Z}/17\mathbb{Z})^{\times}$. Together, Lagrange and Vandermonde isolated the two facts whose tension Galois would resolve fifty years later: resolvents work when the symmetry group has a nice composition series (Vandermonde's success on cyclotomy), and resolvents fail when it does not (Lagrange's degree-6 obstruction for the quintic).

Paolo Ruffini gave an incomplete proof in 1799 that no such formula exists. His 516-page *Teoria generale delle equazioni* attempted to show that no rational function of the roots could serve as a resolvent, but the proof had gaps — notably an incomplete treatment of permutation groups (the concept barely existed). Augustin-Louis Cauchy, who proved key results on permutation groups in 1815 (including that a primitive subgroup of $S_p$ containing a $p$-cycle equals $S_p$), acknowledged Ruffini's priority but did not endorse the proof.

Niels Henrik Abel provided the first rigorous proof in 1824, at age 21. Living in poverty in Norway, Abel could not afford journal publication and self-published a six-page pamphlet (*Mémoire sur les équations algébriques*), compressed to save printing costs, which he sent to leading mathematicians — Gauss reportedly never read it. Abel refined the argument in an 1826 *Journal für die reine und angewandte Mathematik* paper. He died of tuberculosis in 1829 at age 26, two days before a letter arrived offering him a professorship in Berlin.

But it was Évariste Galois who revealed the deeper truth: the solvability of a polynomial is determined by the structure of its symmetry group. His theory explains not just why quintics are unsolvable, but precisely which polynomials can be solved by radicals. Galois submitted his work three times to the Académie des Sciences — Cauchy reviewed the first manuscript (1829) but it was never officially reported, Fourier was sent the second (February 1830) but died in May 1830 before completing his review and the manuscript was lost, and Poisson rejected the third (January 1831) as 'incomprehensible.' Tragically killed in a duel at age 20 in 1832, Galois spent the night before writing a letter to Auguste Chevalier summarizing his theory, with marginal notes including the famous 'je n'ai pas le temps' ('I have not the time').

Galois's manuscripts were finally published by Joseph Liouville in 1846, fourteen years after his death. It took another generation — through the work of Camille Jordan (*Traité des substitutions*, 1870) and others — for the full power of Galois theory to be understood. Today it is fundamental to modern algebra, connecting field extensions to group theory and underpinning algebraic number theory, algebraic geometry, and the Langlands program.
overview.problemStatement:
Theorem (Abel-Ruffini): There is no general solution in radicals to polynomial equations of degree five or higher.

More precisely: there exist polynomials of degree 5 (and higher) whose roots cannot be expressed using only addition, subtraction, multiplication, division, and nth roots applied to the coefficients.

Galois's formulation: A polynomial equation is solvable by radicals if and only if its Galois group is a solvable group.

The symmetric group $S_5$ is not solvable (because the alternating group $A_5$ is simple and non-abelian), so the general quintic, which has Galois group $S_5$, cannot be solved by radicals.
overview.text:
A seven-part pedagogical walkthrough of the Abel-Ruffini theorem (Wiedijk #16) in 187 lines, composing four Mathlib modules with zero sorries and zero axioms. The Galois bridge `galois_bridge` wraps `solvableByRad.isSolvable'` to make explicit the implication: $\alpha$ solvable by radicals $\Rightarrow$ $	ext{Gal}(	ext{minpoly}_F(\alpha))$ solvable. The group-theoretic core `symmetric_group_not_solvable` proves $ orall n \geq 5,\, 
eg\,	ext{IsSolvable}(S_n)$ via `Equiv.Perm.not_solvable` with a `Cardinal.mk (Fin n)` cast bridged by `simp` and `exact_mod_cast`. Instantiations `s5_not_solvable` (via `le_rfl`) and `s6_not_solvable` (via `omega`) provide concrete witnesses, while `a5_is_simple` delegates to `alternatingGroup.isSimpleGroup_five`. The solvable counterparts `s0_solvable` and `s1_solvable` are discharged by `inferInstance`. The synthesis `not_solvable_by_rad_of_not_solvable_gal` combines bridge and obstruction via a 2-line `intro`/`exact` contrapositive: $
eg\,	ext{IsSolvable}(q.	ext{Gal}) \Rightarrow 
eg\,	ext{IsSolvableByRad}\,F\,\alpha$. Nine theorems total, each a pedagogical wrapper over Mathlib infrastructure, organized to mirror the textbook progression from field extensions through group theory to the impossibility conclusion.
overview.proofStrategy:
The proof connects two seemingly unrelated concepts through Galois's fundamental insight:

1. **FIELD EXTENSIONS**: An element $\alpha \in E$ is *solvable by radicals* over $F$ if it lies in a tower $F = K_0 \subset K_1 \subset \cdots \subset K_m \ni \alpha$ where each $K_{i+1} = K_i(\sqrt[n_i]{a_i})$. Mathlib formalizes this as `IsSolvableByRad F α`.

2. **GALOIS GROUPS**: For a polynomial $q(x) \in F[x]$, its Galois group $\text{Gal}(q) \leq S_n$ captures the symmetries of its roots — the automorphisms of the splitting field that fix $F$. Lean represents this as `q.Gal : Type*`.

3. **THE BRIDGE** (`galois_bridge`): $\alpha \in \text{solvableByRad}(F, E) \Rightarrow \text{IsSolvable}(\text{Gal}(\text{minpoly}_F(\alpha)))$. Each radical step $K_i \to K_{i+1} = K_i(\sqrt[n]{a})$ yields a cyclic (hence abelian) Galois group quotient; a group built from abelian quotients is solvable.

4. **GROUP THEORY**: A group $G$ is solvable iff its derived series $G \supset [G,G] \supset [[G,G],[G,G]] \supset \cdots$ reaches $\{e\}$. Crucially:
   - $S_2, S_3, S_4$ are solvable (explaining why quadratics, cubics, quartics have radical formulas)
   - $S_5$ is NOT solvable: $D^1(S_5) = A_5$ and $D^k(S_5) = A_5$ for all $k \geq 1$, because $A_5$ is perfect ($[A_5, A_5] = A_5$, a consequence of its simplicity)

5. **CONCLUSION** (`not_solvable_by_rad_of_not_solvable_gal`): By contrapositive of the bridge, $\neg\,\text{IsSolvable}(\text{Gal}(q)) \Rightarrow \neg\,\text{IsSolvableByRad}\,F\,\alpha$. Since $S_5$ is not solvable and the generic quintic has Galois group $S_5$, the general quintic cannot be solved by radicals. The Lean proof is a 2-line `intro`/`exact`.
keyInsights:
**The Galois Bridge:** `solvableByRad.isSolvable'` captures: $\alpha$ solvable by radicals over $F$ $\Rightarrow$ $\text{Gal}(\text{minpoly}(\alpha))$ solvable. The contrapositive (used in `not_solvable_by_rad_of_not_solvable_gal`) gives the impossibility: $\text{Gal}(q)$ not solvable $\Rightarrow$ roots of $q$ not solvable by radicals.

**Mathlib signature.** The bridge appears in `Mathlib.FieldTheory.AbelRuffini` as `solvableByRad.isSolvable' : Irreducible q → aeval α q = 0 → IsSolvableByRad F α → IsSolvable q.Gal`. Three inputs — irreducibility of $q$, that $\alpha$ is a root, and that $\alpha$ lies in a radical tower over $F$ — combine into a single conclusion about a group-theoretic property of the splitting field. The wrapper `galois_bridge` in `AbelRuffini.lean` (lines 64–67) is a pure renaming: it exposes the Mathlib statement under a name that signposts its conceptual role in the seven-part walkthrough. The wrapper's two-line body `solvableByRad.isSolvable' hq hroot hrad` is the *entire* original content — every mathematical step lives inside `solvableByRad.isSolvable'`.

**Why radicals force solvability (the structural mechanism).** A *radical tower* is a finite chain $F = K_0 \subset K_1 \subset \cdots \subset K_m$ with each step $K_{i+1} = K_i(\sqrt[n_i]{a_i})$ adjoining an $n_i$-th root of some $a_i \in K_i$. If $K_i$ contains the $n_i$-th roots of unity, then $K_{i+1}/K_i$ is a *Kummer extension* and Galois with cyclic Galois group of order dividing $n_i$: the canonical embedding $\text{Gal}(K_{i+1}/K_i) \hookrightarrow \mu_{n_i}$ sends $\sigma \mapsto \sigma(\sqrt[n_i]{a_i})/\sqrt[n_i]{a_i}$, hitting an $n_i$-th root of unity because $(\sigma\sqrt[n_i]{a_i})^{n_i} = \sigma(a_i) = a_i$. When the roots of unity are *not* already present, one adjoins them first via a cyclotomic step: $F \subset F(\zeta_n)$ has Galois group injecting into $(\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z})^\times$, which is abelian. Either way every step has abelian — in fact cyclic — Galois group. The tower's compositum sits inside a Galois closure whose Galois group has a normal series with abelian factors: precisely the definition of a *solvable* group. See [[abel-ruffini-galois-extensions]] for Mathlib's fully composed treatment of solvability across small symmetric groups.

**Why the contrapositive is the operative form.** Mathematically the bridge is an implication $A \Rightarrow B$; for the impossibility result one needs $\neg B \Rightarrow \neg A$. In Lean this is realised by the 2-line proof of `not_solvable_by_rad_of_not_solvable_gal` (`intro hrad; exact hns (galois_bridge α q hq hroot hrad)`): assume the hypothesis the bridge would conclude and discharge with the negation of its premise. The shape `(A → B) → (¬B → ¬A)` is the trivial contrapositive of classical logic — but the *content* is the bridge itself. Every difficulty is hidden inside `solvableByRad.isSolvable'`; the contrapositive is just the wrapping that turns a positive statement (radicals give solvability) into an obstruction (non-solvable groups block radicals).

**The piece the bridge does NOT supply.** The bridge gives impossibility *given* a polynomial whose Galois group is non-solvable. Combined with the non-solvability of $S_5$ (parts III–IV of the file), it reduces Abel-Ruffini to: *exhibit a quintic over $\mathbb{Q}$ with Galois group $S_5$*. That last step — the concrete witness $x^5 - 4x + 2$ with Galois group exactly $S_5$, certified by Eisenstein irreducibility at $p=2$ plus a real-root count of 3 (yielding complex conjugation as a transposition, which together with the 5-cycle from irreducibility generates $S_5$) — is formalised in [[abel-ruffini-oq-04-oq-01]] (0 axioms, 0 sorries). The general theorem `not_solvable_by_rad_of_not_solvable_gal` together with that witness gives the canonical historical statement: $x^5 - 4x + 2 = 0$ has no expression in radicals.

**What Lagrange and Ruffini missed (and why the bridge is the historical pivot).** Lagrange's *Réflexions sur la résolution algébrique des équations* (1770–71) discovered that the *resolvent equations* for degree $n \leq 4$ have lower degree than $n$ (the cubic resolvent of a quartic is a cubic; the resolvent of a cubic is a quadratic) — but the degree-5 resolvent has degree 6, so the reduction strategy collapses. Lagrange saw a symptom; he did not see the underlying group-theoretic obstruction because the language of groups (Galois 1832), normal subgroups, and quotients did not yet exist. Ruffini (1799, with five revisions through 1813) gave a 500-page argument that the quintic resolvent cannot be reduced, but he used an unstated assumption equivalent to: *the radicals appearing in any putative formula must already lie in the splitting field of the polynomial* — what Abel (1824) later isolated as the "Abel-Galois lemma". The bridge `solvableByRad.isSolvable'`, in its modern form, makes that lemma the *content* of the implication: tower-membership pulls back into a group-theoretic property of the splitting field. Until that pull-back was made rigorous, the impossibility could not be proved — only conjectured. See [[inverse-galois]] for the converse direction (which Galois groups can arise as $\text{Gal}(K/\mathbb{Q})$; the bridge as stated cannot be reversed in general).

**Sharpness.** The bridge is one-way: a solvable Galois group does *not* automatically imply solvable by radicals over $\mathbb{Q}$ without further hypotheses on roots of unity in the base. Over fields of characteristic $p$ dividing the relevant orders, Kummer theory breaks; the Artin-Schreier substitute uses extensions of the form $K(\alpha)$ with $\alpha^p - \alpha = a$, and a generalised "solvable by radicals plus Artin-Schreier" notion is needed for the full converse. Mathlib's `IsSolvableByRad` and `solvableByRad.isSolvable'` are stated so that the Abel-Ruffini direction — what `not_solvable_by_rad_of_not_solvable_gal` proves — survives in full generality: non-solvable Galois group blocks radical expressibility regardless of characteristic, root-of-unity availability, or base field. The converse (Galois's positive theorem: every solvable Galois group is realised by a radical tower over a characteristic-zero base, once a sufficient root of unity is adjoined) is the *other* half of the equivalence Galois conjectured and which Mathlib develops separately.

**Degree 5 Threshold via Derived Series:** $S_4$ has derived length 3: $D^1(S_4) = A_4$, $D^2(S_4) = V_4$, $D^3(S_4) = \{e\}$ (since $V_4$ is abelian). A composition series (refining the derived series) is $S_4 \supset A_4 \supset V_4 \supset \langle(12)(34)\rangle \supset \{e\}$ with cyclic prime-order quotients. Contrast with $S_5$: $D^k(S_5) = A_5$ for all $k \geq 1$ (stuck — $A_5$ is perfect: $[A_5,A_5] = A_5$). This is why degree 4 has a radical formula but degree 5 does not.

**A₅ is the Key Obstruction:** $|A_5| = 60$, $A_5$ is the smallest non-abelian simple group. `alternatingGroup.isSimpleGroup_five` formalizes this. The Klein four-group $V_4 = \{e,(12)(34),(13)(24),(14)(23)\}$ makes $A_4$ solvable; no analog exists in $A_5$. **Conjugacy-class arithmetic of $A_5$ — the concrete simplicity certificate.** The 60 elements of $A_5$ partition into exactly 5 conjugacy classes with sizes $1 + 20 + 15 + 12 + 12 = 60$: the identity (1 element), the 3-cycles like $(1\,2\,3)$ (20 elements = $\binom{5}{3} \cdot 2$), the double-transpositions like $(1\,2)(3\,4)$ (15 elements = $\binom{5}{2}\binom{3}{2}/2$), and the 5-cycles which *split* in $A_5$ into two classes of 12 each ($24/2$ — the standard cycle $(1\,2\,3\,4\,5)$ is not $A_5$-conjugate to $(1\,2\,3\,5\,4)$ because conjugating by $(4\,5) \notin A_5$ would be required). A normal subgroup $N \triangleleft A_5$ must be a union of conjugacy classes containing $\{e\}$, so $|N|$ must be a sum starting with $1$ chosen from $\{1, 20, 15, 12, 12\}$ — *and* must divide 60 (Lagrange). Exhaustive check: $1, 1+12=13, 1+15=16, 1+20=21, 1+12+12=25, 1+15+12=28, 1+15+20=36, 1+12+12+15=40, 1+12+12+20=45, 1+15+12+20=48$, all the way up to $1+15+12+12+20=60$ — only $1$ and $60$ divide $60$. Hence the only normal subgroups are $\{e\}$ and $A_5$ itself: simple. This is the *direct* simplicity proof that bypasses Sylow theory entirely; the Sylow-counting alternative ($n_2 = 5, n_3 = 10, n_5 = 6$, none equal to 1, hence no normal Sylow subgroup) is formalized in the sub-entries `sylow-theorem-oq-04` and `sylow-theorems-oq-04`. The 5-cycle class-splitting phenomenon ($1$ class of 24 in $S_5$ becomes 2 classes of 12 in $A_5$) is the same arithmetic obstruction that makes the icosahedral dessin (with monodromy $A_5$) rigid under the absolute Galois action (cf. openQuestion on dessins d'enfants), tying the local conjugacy-class structure to the global Grothendieck-Teichmüller setting.

**Ferrari's Resolvent Cubic as $S_4 / V_4 \cong S_3$: The Concrete Bridge from Classical Formula to Galois Theory.** Ferrari's 1545 quartic formula reduces the quartic $x^4 + px^2 + qx + r$ to a *resolvent cubic* — a cubic equation in an auxiliary variable whose roots, once known, complete the quartic by two further square-root extractions. The Galois-theoretic explanation, due to Lagrange-Galois, is exact: the Klein four-group $V_4 \trianglelefteq S_4$ is *normal* (in fact characteristic), the quotient $S_4 / V_4$ is isomorphic to $S_3$, and the resolvent cubic is precisely the polynomial whose splitting field is the $V_4$-fixed subfield. Concretely, if $r_1, r_2, r_3, r_4$ are the roots of the quartic, the three quantities $y_1 = (r_1 + r_2)(r_3 + r_4)$, $y_2 = (r_1 + r_3)(r_2 + r_4)$, $y_3 = (r_1 + r_4)(r_2 + r_3)$ are permuted by $S_4$ through its $V_4$-quotient, hence form the roots of a cubic with rational coefficients — Ferrari's resolvent. The full quartic Galois chain $\mathbb{Q} \subset \mathbb{Q}(y_1, y_2, y_3) \subset \mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{D}, y_i) \subset \mathbb{Q}(r_1, \ldots, r_4)$ matches the composition series $S_4 \supset A_4 \supset V_4 \supset \{e\}$ step-for-step: $S_4 / A_4 \cong \mathbb{Z}/2$ adjoins $\sqrt{D}$ (the discriminant), $A_4 / V_4 \cong \mathbb{Z}/3$ adjoins the cube root in Cardano's solution of the resolvent, and $V_4 / \{e\} \cong (\mathbb{Z}/2)^2$ adjoins the two final square roots. This explains *why* the quartic formula is exactly four nested radicals (one square, one cube, two squares) — they correspond bijectively to the composition factors of $S_4$. The failure at degree 5 is now diagnosable with surgical precision: $S_5$ contains no normal subgroup of index $\leq 5$ except $A_5$ (which is simple non-abelian), so no analogue of Ferrari's $V_4$-trick exists — there is no normal subgroup whose quotient is a smaller solvable symmetric group. The quintic's resolvent (Lagrange 1770) has degree 6, *higher* than the original, instead of lower — the first historical hint that the strategy must fail.

**Mathlib Integration Pattern — Four Modules Compose Into Nine Wrappers:** The 187-line file delegates the entire mathematical content of Abel-Ruffini to four Mathlib modules, then exposes nine theorem-shaped views onto that content with proofs that average under two lines. The dependency picture: `Mathlib.FieldTheory.AbelRuffini` supplies the single Galois bridge `solvableByRad.isSolvable'` ($\alpha$ solvable by radicals over $F$ and $q$ irreducible with $q(\alpha) = 0$ $\Rightarrow$ $\text{Gal}(q)$ solvable), whose internal proof is itself ~2000 lines spanning splitting-field constructions, Kummer theory at each radical layer, and the cyclotomic + cyclic decomposition of solvable groups (see keyInsights #12 and #25 on Hilbert's Satz 90); `Mathlib.GroupTheory.Solvable` supplies the `IsSolvable` predicate (a wrapper around `Group.derivedSeries G n = ⊥` for some $n$) plus `Equiv.Perm.not_solvable` (the structural $S_n$-non-solvability result, transcribed from Burnside-style derived-series analysis); `Mathlib.GroupTheory.SpecificGroups.Alternating` supplies `alternatingGroup.isSimpleGroup_five` (the simplicity of $A_5$ via Sylow counting and conjugacy-class arithmetic — see keyInsight #2 and the `sylow-theorems-oq-04` cross-reference); `Mathlib.FieldTheory.Galois.Basic` supplies the `Polynomial.Gal` type and the `IsSolvable` instance machinery that makes the Galois group of a polynomial typeclass-discoverable. The compositional pattern is uniform: `galois_bridge` is a one-line term-mode wrapper of `solvableByRad.isSolvable'`; `symmetric_group_not_solvable` adds only a two-line `Cardinal.mk (Fin n) ≥ 5` bridge before calling `Equiv.Perm.not_solvable`; `s5_not_solvable`/`s6_not_solvable` are one-line specializations at $n = 5, 6$ via `le_rfl`/`omega`; `a5_is_simple` is a one-line definitional wrapper; `s0_solvable`/`s1_solvable` are discharged by `inferInstance` (Mathlib already knows trivial groups are solvable); and the load-bearing `not_solvable_by_rad_of_not_solvable_gal` is the two-line contrapositive `intro hrad; exact hns (galois_bridge α q hq hroot hrad)`. The net effect is that the file's *logical content* (zero sorries, zero axioms in 187 lines) is essentially nine carefully-chosen *names* attached to the right Mathlib lemmas — an architecture that lets the gallery present Abel-Ruffini at textbook granularity (Parts I–VII, one theorem per concept) without re-implementing any of the underlying field- and group-theoretic infrastructure. This is the canonical template for Mathlib-backed gallery entries: substantive *organization* and *exposition* layered over a foundation whose mathematical weight is honestly attributed to upstream Mathlib in the `badge: "mathlib"` and `assumptions` fields.

**S_n Unsolvability for n ≥ 5:** `symmetric_group_not_solvable` proves $\forall n \geq 5$, $S_n$ not solvable, using `Cardinal.mk (Fin n) ≥ 5` via `simp`. Instances for $S_0, S_1$ (`inferInstance`) vs the impossibility for $S_5, S_6, \ldots$ illustrate the sharp boundary. **The structural mechanism inside `Equiv.Perm.not_solvable`** reduces every $n \geq 5$ case to the simplicity of $A_5$: it embeds a 5-element subset's symmetric group $S_5 \hookrightarrow \mathrm{Sym}(X)$ as a subgroup, then invokes the closure of solvability under subgroups (`IsSolvable.subgroupOf`) — if $S_X$ were solvable, every subgroup of $S_X$ including the copy of $S_5$ would be solvable too, contradicting the non-solvability of $S_5$. **The witnessing obstruction inside $S_5$ is the *perfect* subgroup $A_5$**: since $A_5$ is non-abelian simple, its commutator subgroup is $A_5$ itself ($[A_5, A_5] = A_5$, the defining property of a perfect group), so the derived series of $S_5$ collapses to $S_5 \trianglerighteq A_5 \trianglerighteq A_5 \trianglerighteq \cdots$ — stabilizing at $A_5$ and never reaching $\{e\}$, the textbook definition of non-solvability. **Degree 5 is Necessary but Not Sufficient — The $X^5 - 2$ vs $x^5 - 4x + 2$ Dichotomy.** A common misreading of Abel-Ruffini is that 'no quintic is solvable by radicals'. The gallery makes the precise statement concrete with two degree-5 polynomials whose Galois groups land on opposite sides of the solvability threshold. (i) $\text{Gal}(X^5 - 2/\mathbb{Q}) \cong F_{20} = \mathbb{Z}/5 \rtimes \mathbb{Z}/4$ (Frobenius group of order 20), formalized in `inverse-galois-f20`. $F_{20}$ is solvable — derived series $F_{20} \supset \mathbb{Z}/5 \supset \{e\}$ with abelian quotients $\mathbb{Z}/4$ and $\mathbb{Z}/5$ — so $X^5 - 2$ *is* solvable by radicals; the explicit root is $\sqrt[5]{2}$. (ii) $\text{Gal}(x^5 - 4x + 2/\mathbb{Q}) \cong S_5$, formalized in `abel-ruffini-oq-04-oq-01` via Eisenstein at $p = 2$ and `galActionHom` bijectivity. $S_5$ is non-solvable, so the roots of $x^5 - 4x + 2$ are *not* expressible by radicals. Same degree (5), opposite outcomes, decided entirely by group structure — neither degree alone nor irreducibility alone determines radical solvability. The discriminating invariant is the Galois group, which is precisely what `not_solvable_by_rad_of_not_solvable_gal` takes as its key hypothesis. A third gallery instance, `inverse-galois-d4` ($\text{Gal}(X^4 - 2/\mathbb{Q}) \cong D_4$, solvable), confirms the same principle one degree down: $X^4 - 2$ has solvable Galois group, hence solvable by radicals via $\sqrt[4]{2}$.

**Transitive Subgroups of $S_5$: The Five Possible Galois Groups for an Irreducible Quintic.** For any irreducible $f \in \mathbb{Q}[X]$ of degree 5, $\text{Gal}(f/\mathbb{Q})$ acts faithfully and transitively on the 5 roots (irreducibility is equivalent to transitivity), hence embeds as a transitive subgroup of $S_5$. Up to conjugacy in $S_5$ there are exactly five such subgroups: $C_5$ (order 5, cyclic), $D_5$ (order 10, dihedral), $F_{20} = \text{AGL}(1, \mathbb{F}_5) = \mathbb{Z}/5 \rtimes \mathbb{Z}/4$ (Frobenius group, order 20), $A_5$ (order 60), and $S_5$ (order 120). The first three contain $C_5$ as a normal subgroup with abelian quotient, so they are solvable; $A_5$ is simple non-abelian, so $A_5$ and $S_5$ are not. The dichotomy of keyInsight #8 ($X^5 - 2$ vs $x^5 - 4x + 2$) is therefore the simplest non-trivial instance of a discrete 3-vs-2 classification: the Galois group of an irreducible quintic lands in one of $\{C_5, D_5, F_{20}\}$ (radically expressible) or one of $\{A_5, S_5\}$ (not). Concretely, $\text{Gal}(X^5 - 2/\mathbb{Q}) = F_{20}$ and $\text{Gal}(x^5 - 4x + 2/\mathbb{Q}) = S_5$ are neighbours in the lattice of transitive subgroups, separated only by the solvable/non-solvable line. Identifying which of the five a given quintic produces is the goal of resolvent-based algorithms (Cayley's resolvent sextic, Dummit's 1991 resolvents) and is implemented in modern computer-algebra systems (Magma's `GaloisGroup`, SageMath's `NumberField.galois_group`, PARI/GP `polgalois`). The analogous classification at degree 4 has five transitive subgroups of $S_4$ ($\mathbb{Z}/4, V_4, D_4, A_4, S_4$) — all solvable, matching the existence of Ferrari's quartic formula; this is precisely why $n = 5$ is the smallest degree where the classification *contains* non-solvable groups.

**Jordan-Hölder Guarantees Completeness:** The analysis of $S_n$ via derived series is not ad hoc — the Jordan-Hölder theorem guarantees that any two composition series of a finite group have the same multiset of composition factors (up to isomorphism). For $S_5$, the unique composition series is $\{e\} \triangleleft A_5 \triangleleft S_5$ with factors $A_5$ (simple, order 60) and $\mathbb{Z}/2$. Since $A_5$ is non-abelian, the group is not solvable — and no alternative decomposition can avoid this obstruction. This uniqueness is what makes the degree-5 boundary absolute rather than a limitation of one particular analysis.

**Discriminant Criterion and the $x^5 - x - 1$ Recipe for $\text{Gal} = S_5$:** The theorem `not_solvable_by_rad_of_not_solvable_gal` requires exhibiting a polynomial with non-solvable Galois group. The standard recipe for $f = x^5 - x - 1$ assembles three independent ingredients into $\text{Gal}(f/\mathbb{Q}) = S_5$. (i) **Irreducibility over $\mathbb{Q}$** (Selmer 1956): $f$ is irreducible — the canonical witness in this entry's references. Irreducibility forces $\text{Gal}(f)$ to act transitively on the five roots, so $|\text{Gal}(f)|$ is divisible by 5; by Cauchy's theorem, $\text{Gal}(f)$ contains an element of order 5 — a 5-cycle (the only order-5 element type in $S_5$). Note this 5-cycle comes from *irreducibility over $\mathbb{Q}$ + Cauchy*, not from the number of real roots — a common conflation. (ii) **Discriminant criterion**: $\Delta(f) = 2869 = 19 \times 151$ is not a perfect square in $\mathbb{Q}$, and $\text{Gal}(f) \subseteq A_n$ iff $\Delta(f) \in (F^*)^2$, so $\text{Gal}(f) \not\subseteq A_5$. This means $\text{Gal}(f)$ contains an *odd* permutation. (iii) **Complex conjugation as a transposition**: a Sturm-sequence analysis (or graphing) of $f$ shows it has exactly 3 real roots and 2 non-real roots forming a complex-conjugate pair. Complex conjugation, restricted to $\text{Gal}(f) \subseteq S_5$, fixes the 3 real roots and swaps the 2 non-real ones — a transposition. **Synthesis**: $\text{Gal}(f)$ is a transitive subgroup of $S_5$ containing both a 5-cycle and a transposition. By a classical theorem (Galois 1830), the only transitive subgroup of $S_5$ containing both a 5-cycle and a transposition is $S_5$ itself. Hence $\text{Gal}(f) = S_5$. (Once a 5-cycle and a transposition are present, ingredient ii is technically redundant — the transitive 5-cycle/transposition criterion alone forces $S_5$.) Formalizing this three-ingredient recipe in Lean would bridge the gap between the abstract `not_solvable_by_rad_of_not_solvable_gal` and a concrete unsolvable quintic; the alternative `abel-ruffini-oq-04-oq-01` formalization uses the Eisenstein-at-$p=2$ + galActionHom path on $x^5 - 4x + 2$ instead, but the conceptual recipe is the same: irreducibility (5-cycle by Cauchy) + non-real roots (transposition by complex conjugation) generate $S_5$ as a transitive subgroup.

**Roots of Unity as the Engine of Radical Extensions:** Every radical step $K_i \to K_i(\sqrt[n]{a})$ implicitly requires the $n$th roots of unity $\zeta_n = e^{2\pi i/n}$. The cyclotomic extension $\mathbb{Q}(\zeta_n)/\mathbb{Q}$ has Galois group $(\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z})^{\times}$, which is abelian (hence solvable). This is the hidden ingredient in the Galois bridge: each radical step contributes an abelian Galois quotient precisely because the underlying cyclotomic symmetries are abelian (by De Moivre's formula, the $n$th roots of unity form a cyclic group under multiplication). The Abel-Ruffini impossibility arises when the polynomial's Galois group $S_5$ cannot be decomposed into such abelian layers — a failure of solvability that no choice of radical tower can circumvent.

**Kummer Theory Powers Each Radical Step:** Why is each radical extension's Galois group cyclic in the first place? Kummer theory (developed in the 1840s for cyclotomic fields, generalized by Helmut Hasse in the 1920s and reformulated cohomologically by Tate): for a field $K$ containing a primitive $n$th root of unity (with $\text{char}(K) \nmid n$), the cyclic Galois extensions of $K$ with exponent dividing $n$ correspond bijectively to subgroups of $K^*/(K^*)^n$. Concretely, $K(\sqrt[n]{a})/K$ has cyclic Galois group $\mathbb{Z}/d$ where $d$ is the order of $a$ in $K^*/(K^*)^n$. This is the precise structural fact behind the Galois bridge: a radical tower $F = K_0 \subset K_1 \subset \cdots \subset K_m$ gives composition factors that are all cyclic (after adjoining the necessary roots of unity), so the resulting Galois group is solvable. The contrapositive — non-solvable $\text{Gal}(q)$ admits no Kummer-style decomposition into cyclic radical layers — is the structural reason no radical formula can exist for the generic quintic. Mathlib's `solvableByRad.isSolvable'` packages this entire chain (Kummer correspondence + composition series + cyclotomic abelianness) into a single hypothesis-discharging step. The constructive converse (solvable Galois group $\Rightarrow$ explicit radical tower) is precisely the Kummer-theoretic procedure: at each composition factor $G_{i}/G_{i+1} \cong \mathbb{Z}/n_i$, the Kummer correspondence supplies the radical $\sqrt[n_i]{a_i}$ that generates the corresponding cyclic extension.

**Abel-Ruffini is Radical-Specific, Not Formula-Specific:** The impossibility is precisely about the four operations $\{+, -, \times, \div, \sqrt[n]{\,}\}$. Hermite (1858) showed the general quintic IS solvable using elliptic modular functions: via the icosahedral substitution $z \mapsto j(\tau)$ (the $j$-invariant), the quintic's five roots can be expressed in terms of hypergeometric series and theta functions. Klein's 1884 *Lectures on the Icosahedron* developed this fully, connecting the icosahedral symmetry group $A_5 \cong I_{60}$ to $j(\tau)$ via the relation $j(\tau) = \frac{(12g_2)^3}{\Delta}$ (with $\Delta$ the discriminant of the elliptic curve). The gallery sub-entry `abel-ruffini-oq-04-oq-07` formalizes the preparatory Bring-Jerrard reduction ($x^5 + x + t = 0$) and the Bring radical — the first step toward the elliptic solution. This insight clarifies the conceptual stakes: proving Abel-Ruffini tells us exactly *which* vocabulary of operations fails; using larger vocabularies (transcendental functions, Puiseux series, differential equations) restores solvability at the cost of leaving the radical framework.

**Arnold's Topological Proof (1963)**: Vladimir Arnold gave a completely different proof of Abel-Ruffini using the fundamental group. A radical formula for the quintic would define a continuous multi-valued function from the coefficient space $\mathbb{C}^5$ to the roots, factoring through branched covers corresponding to radical extractions. The monodromy of this function around the discriminant locus would give a solvable subgroup of the braid group, contradicting the fact that the full monodromy is $S_5$. This topological approach, made rigorous by Khovanskii (1970s-80s) via topological Galois theory, requires no algebra — only the fundamental group of configuration spaces.

**Lagrange Resolvent as Discrete Fourier Transform**: Lagrange's 1770 resolvent — the central technique behind Cardano's cubic formula and Ferrari's quartic — is, in modern language, a discrete Fourier transform over a cyclic group. Given roots $r_1, \ldots, r_n$ of a polynomial whose Galois group has a normal subgroup of cyclic quotient $\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}$, the Lagrange resolvent $\langle \zeta, \beta\rangle = \sum_{k=0}^{n-1} \zeta^k \sigma^k(\beta)$ (with $\zeta$ a primitive $n$th root of unity and $\sigma$ a generator of the cyclic quotient) diagonalizes the action: by orthogonality of characters of $\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}$, the resolvent's $n$th power is fixed by the cyclic action and therefore lies in the smaller field. This is precisely the discrete Fourier inversion formula, $\hat{f}(\zeta) \hat{f}(\zeta^{-1}) \in F$ for $\hat{f}$ the DFT of a function on $\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}$. Vandermonde's 1771 solution of $x^{11} - 1 = 0$ is the textbook instance: he computed the discrete Fourier transform of the eleven roots over the cyclic group $(\mathbb{Z}/11\mathbb{Z})^{\times}$. The Abel-Ruffini obstruction can therefore be rephrased: there is no DFT-style decomposition of the action of a non-solvable group like $S_5$ into cyclic pieces, because $A_5$ is perfect — no abelian quotient exists to define an analog of $\zeta$. Modern fast-Fourier-transform algorithms (Cooley-Tukey 1965) implement exactly the radical-tower structure that Galois theory shows is unavailable for non-solvable Galois groups.
